boards.title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
boards.description: Ten documented University of Florida rituals, songs, events and symbols that frame Gator gatherings.

cards.title: Make the Gator Chomp
cards.subtitle: UF game-day tradition
cards.notes: At a game or rally, place your right arm over your left and chomp along when the band plays the Jaws theme before kickoff.
cards.short_summary: A coordinated alligator-arm gesture used in Gator sports settings.
cards.evidence_claim: UF Student Life identifies the Gator Chomp as a Florida tradition, traditionally used before every kickoff with the Jaws theme.
cards.access_notes: Follow event staff and venue guidance when attending athletics events.

cards.title: Stand Up for Mr. Two Bits
cards.subtitle: Pre-game cheer at UF home football
cards.notes: Listen for the pre-game call, then join the simple arm-circle motion and final raised arm if you are attending a home football game.
cards.short_summary: A pre-game call-and-response linked to longtime fan George Edmondson.
cards.evidence_claim: UF Student Life says the Mr. Two Bits Cheer is said before the start of each home football game.
cards.access_notes: The cheer is part of home-football pre-game programming.

cards.title: Sway Through “We Are the Boys”
cards.subtitle: End-of-third-quarter football ritual
cards.notes: At the third-quarter break, stand with nearby fans, link shoulders when welcome, and sway left to right while singing the traditional song.
cards.short_summary: The stadium-wide third-quarter singalong and sway.
cards.evidence_claim: UF Student Life describes fans standing, putting arms around neighbors’ shoulders and singing while swaying after the third quarter of every home game.
cards.access_notes: Participate only with consent and respect the space of people around you.

cards.title: Sing the Alma Mater After a Win
cards.subtitle: Football postgame song tradition
cards.notes: After a home win, stay through the final whistle and listen as the team, coaches, fans and band gather for the Alma Mater.
cards.short_summary: A post-win gathering around UF’s official school song.
cards.evidence_claim: UF Student Life states that the Alma Mater is performed at commencements and after home football wins with the team, coaches, fans and band.
cards.access_notes: The post-win football performance depends on the game result.

cards.title: Learn “The Orange and Blue”
cards.subtitle: UF fight-song tradition
cards.notes: Use the official Student Life lyrics to follow the fight song at athletics events, rallies or other organized Gator gatherings.
cards.short_summary: UF’s fight song centers on cheering for the Orange and Blue.
cards.evidence_claim: UF Student Life publishes “The Fight Song” lyrics as part of its UF traditions chants-and-cheers guide.
cards.access_notes: Follow the program cues at the event you attend.

cards.title: Answer “Orange” with “Blue”
cards.subtitle: Stadium call-and-response
cards.notes: At football or basketball, listen for the split-stadium chant: the east side calls “Orange” and the west side responds “Blue.”
cards.short_summary: A venue-wide Orange/Blue call-and-response used at Gator games.
cards.evidence_claim: UF Student Life says the east and west sides of the stadium trade “Orange” and “Blue,” most commonly during football and basketball games.
cards.access_notes: Participation is tied to athletics-event programming.

cards.title: See Gator Growl’s Homecoming Ritual
cards.subtitle: Student-led pep rally
cards.notes: Check UF Homecoming programming for the current edition of this student-led pep rally, historically scheduled before the Homecoming football game.
cards.short_summary: A Homecoming pep rally introduced by Florida Blue Key in 1923.
cards.evidence_claim: UF News reports that Florida Blue Key added the student-run Gator Growl to Homecoming festivities in 1923 as a pep rally before kickoff.
cards.source_title: Gator Growl turns 100. Here's a look at the past 10 decades
cards.access_notes: Event format, location and admission can change; consult current Homecoming information.

cards.title: Watch the Homecoming Parade
cards.subtitle: Annual Homecoming-week procession
cards.notes: Look for the announced parade route during Homecoming Week and watch the student-organization floats from a lawful public viewing spot.
cards.short_summary: A themed float parade with roots in UF’s early Homecoming history.
cards.evidence_claim: UF News says the Fightin’ Gator Marching Band led the first Homecoming parade in 1916 and that student organizations later decorated floats.
cards.source_title: Gator Growl turns 100. Here's a look at the past 10 decades
cards.access_notes: Route, timing and viewing access are set annually by Homecoming organizers.

cards.title: Recognize the Gator Wrap
cards.subtitle: Student and alumni ring tradition
cards.notes: View the Alumni Association’s ring history and design before deciding whether this long-running student-and-alumni tradition is meaningful to you.
cards.short_summary: A distinctive UF ring tradition dating to the late 1930s.
cards.evidence_claim: The UF Alumni Association says the Gator Wrap has been a tradition among UF students and alumni since the late 1930s.
cards.access_notes: A ring is optional merchandise; consult the official program for current ordering details.

cards.title: Spot the Holiday Gator
cards.subtitle: Seasonal orange-and-blue campus installation
cards.notes: During the winter holiday season, check UF announcements before visiting the University Auditorium lawn to view the illuminated steel alligator.
cards.short_summary: A seasonal campus sculpture tradition that began in 2019.
cards.evidence_claim: UF News described the Holiday Gator as a new annual tradition: an orange-and-blue illuminated steel alligator near University Auditorium.
cards.source_title: Holiday Gator to return to UF
cards.access_notes: Seasonal display dates and installation status should be verified with current UF announcements.
